strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: forecasting pre-training loss from early checkpoints. Its reciprocal model of loss across token positions offers an interpretable empirical description.

The experiments provide promising evidence across two model sizes trained for 400B tokens and two evaluation distributions. The reported positional fits achieve R² > 0.95 for over 99% of checkpoints, and Figure 1 reports substantially lower forecasting errors than the selected baselines.

The position-weighting experiments extend the investigation beyond curve fitting, evaluating three interventions on eight benchmarks under zero-, one-, and five-shot settings. They provide useful evidence that these particular interventions yield similar aggregate performance.
weaknesses: The forecasting evaluation does not clearly separate discovering the law from testing it. Section 3.3 selects the transition point using overall fit quality across training trajectories, while Section 3.4 evaluates forecasts from their early prefixes. The manuscript does not establish that the functional forms and transition point were fixed independently of the forecast targets. Independent trajectories or a strictly prefix-only selection protocol are needed to substantiate the central predictive claim.

The baselines do not isolate the contribution of token-position modeling. The proposed method incorporates the known cosine learning-rate schedule, whereas the comparison functions do not. Once a0 and a1 are constant, Equation 10 reduces to average loss = a2(N) + a constant. A direct schedule-aware fit to average loss is therefore an essential missing baseline. Without this ablation, the reported improvements cannot establish that the positional decomposition improves forecasting.

The conclusion that position-based reweighting is unnecessary exceeds the evidence. Equal observed loss decreases under one objective do not establish equal optimization difficulty or exclude benefits from other objectives. Three suppression schemes, introduced only after 100B tokens, cannot settle this broader claim. Table 2 also lacks uncertainty estimates or repeated runs; for example, tail suppression slightly improves the smaller model's average score. The supported conclusion is limited to similar performance for the tested interventions.

Reproducibility is insufficiently documented. The referenced appendix containing fitting parameters is absent from the supplied manuscript. Nonlinear fitting procedures, initialization and constraints, batch size needed to convert warmup steps into tokens, and weighting normalization are unspecified. The transition point is also inconsistent: Section 3.3 gives two-fifths of training, which would be 160B tokens, while Section 4.1 states 120B. This directly affects reproducing the forecasts.

Generality is demonstrated only within two related model sizes, one training corpus, one 400B-token budget, and one learning-rate schedule. Evaluating on PG-19 adds distributional coverage but does not test transfer across optimization schedules or training budgets. The proposed applications to hyperparameter selection, data-mixture selection, and early stopping remain untested.

The novelty and theoretical motivation need more precise framing. Kaplan et al. already studied loss versus training steps, so describing temporal training behavior as previously untouched is overstated. Equation 5 also does not generally hold for individual successive tokens merely because context grows; an expected conditional-entropy argument requires additional assumptions. These issues warrant presenting the contribution as an empirical, schedule-conditioned model.
